job.style: a passage that shows a common wrong method and corrects it

passage: When plotting a linear relation on a Cartesian plane, students often make mistakes by misunderstanding the axes. Some think the origin is simply the bottom-left corner of the grid, but it is actually the intersection where the x-axis and y-axis meet at (0,0). Another common error occurs when plotting coordinates like (1, 4). A student might mistakenly count 4 units up and 1 unit across, forgetting that the first number represents the x-coordinate, which dictates horizontal movement from the origin. Furthermore, when drawing a linear graph, some students incorrectly believe the line should stop exactly at the last plotted point. In reality, a linear relation represents a continuous pattern, so the line must extend beyond the plotted points to show it continues infinitely. Finally, when connecting points, some students try to draw a wavy curve through them. This is incorrect; because the relation is linear, you must use a straight edge to draw a single straight line that passes through all the points. By following these rules—starting from the origin, correctly identifying coordinates, and extending straight lines—you can accurately represent mathematical relationships on a graph.

items.evidence: Some think the origin is simply the bottom-left corner of the grid, but it is actually the intersection where the x-axis and y-axis meet at (0,0).
items.q: On Meena's graph, the x-axis and y-axis meet near the page centre. Where is the origin?
options: At the crossing point of both axes
At the bottom-left corner of the page
At the top-right corner of the page
At the point where the x-axis ends
items.explain: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis meet at (0,0), not a page corner.

wrong.why: thinks the origin is always the bottom-left corner
thinks counting starts from the top right
thinks the origin is where an axis ends

items.evidence: A student might mistakenly count 4 units up and 1 unit across, forgetting that the first number represents the x-coordinate, which dictates horizontal movement from the origin.
items.q: How should you move to plot the point (1, 4)?
options: Move 1 right and 4 up from page corner
Move 1 right and 4 up from last point
items.explain: The first number is the x-coordinate, so move 1 across from the origin, then 4 up.

wrong.why: thinks the first number tells how far up
thinks the origin is the bottom-left corner
counts from where the pencil is, not the origin

items.evidence: In reality, a linear relation represents a continuous pattern, so the line must extend beyond the plotted points to show it continues infinitely.
items.q: Why does the line of a linear graph not stop at the last plotted point?
options: Because the pattern continues past the points
Because longer lines are easier to read
Because the last point may be plotted wrong
Because every line must reach the origin
items.explain: A linear relation is a continuous pattern, so the line extends to show it goes on forever.

wrong.why: thinks extending is only for neatness
invents a reason about plotting errors
mixes up extending the line with starting from the origin

items.evidence: This is incorrect; because the relation is linear, you must use a straight edge to draw a single straight line that passes through all the points.
items.q: Asha has plotted three points of a linear relation. How should she join them?
options: With one straight line drawn using a ruler
With a smooth wavy curve through each point
With short separate lines between each pair
With a straight line through only two points
items.explain: A linear relation needs one straight line, drawn with a straight edge, through all the points.

wrong.why: thinks the graph should rise and fall like a hill
thinks each pair of points is joined separately
forgets the line must pass through all points
